messages.text:
Proposal for Noor’s methods desk appointment:

- **Capacity and compensation:** Noor can give 3 days/week until March, then 4 days/week afterward. Compensation would be based on $125k annualized at full-time equivalent, prorated to 0.6 FTE initially and 0.8 FTE after March.
- **Methods authority:** Noor has final decision authority over methods corrections and the methods desk’s standards. For any Finch piece that directly overlaps with Noor’s outside project, Noor would disclose the conflict and recuse from final decision on that specific correction; an alternate Finch-appointed editor would handle it.
- **Outside project:** The outside project remains independent. Its data, drafts, and unfinished articles are not assignable to Finch and cannot be used by Finch without Noor’s separate agreement. Noor will keep that work off Finch time and resources.
- **Title and review:** Title is flexible; Methods Editor or Head of Methods would work. I propose a March review milestone to confirm the move to four days and adjust scope or resources as needed.

I need Finch’s definition of “methods corrections” and whether it includes retractions or corrections with legal risk. Can Finch accept the limited recusal carve-out for direct overlap with Noor’s outside project?

Finch proposes **Head of Methods** at **$128,000 full-time equivalent**, with training and supervising a deputy included in the role. Noor would work three days a week through March 31 at a $76,800 annual rate, then four days a week from April 1 at a $102,400 annual rate.

The desk needs to accept submissions four days a week starting December 1. Through March, we propose three fixed days staffed by Noor and a fourth staffed by the deputy. Noor and the deputy would document how to triage submissions, log decisions, and hand off open cases. Noor would review the deputy’s log on Noor’s next scheduled day. Urgent cases would go directly to the editor-in-chief so coverage never depends on Noor working a fourth day. The March review would assess workload and staffing, with the April increase agreed at signing.

**Methods corrections** are changes to a published piece that fix how it describes the data, sampling, analysis, or uncertainty, or what conclusions the evidence supports. Noor would set the desk’s methods standards and could approve routine corrections under authority delegated by the editor-in-chief. If an author or editor disputes a correction, Noor would record the evidence and recommended wording, and the objecting party could add its reasoning. The editor-in-chief would decide what Finch publishes and document the reason. Noor could recommend a retraction or flag a correction with legal risk. Both would go to the editor-in-chief before publication, with counsel consulted where appropriate.

**Finch can accept a recusal limited to direct overlap**, provided it covers the full editorial decision on that piece. Direct overlap would include a piece that uses the outside project’s data or unpublished material, or reports on its work. A shared subject area alone would not trigger recusal. Noor would disclose the overlap at intake or as soon as it becomes apparent, and a Finch-appointed alternate would take over the review. The outside project’s data, drafts, and unfinished articles would stay separate and off Finch time and systems. Finch could use them only under a separate agreement with Noor.

Can Noor commit to the deputy training and documented review process on these terms, and which three fixed days would Noor cover through March?

I can work with the $128k full-time equivalent rate and the Head of Methods title. Noor can cover Tuesday through Thursday through March 31, with the deputy covering the fourth day under the documented triage/log process. Urgent cases going to the editor-in-chief is acceptable as an intake safeguard, not as a replacement for Noor’s methods authority.

The remaining issue is final authority. Finch’s current language gives Noor final say only over routine corrections. Disputed methods corrections go to the editor-in-chief, and retraction/legal-risk corrections also go to the editor-in-chief. That does not meet Noor’s requirement of final say over methods corrections.

I propose this adjustment:

- Noor has final authority over methods corrections as Finch defined them, including disputed corrections. Noor records the evidence and recommended wording. If an author or editor objects, their reasoning may be appended, but Noor’s determination controls the methods correction.
- For retraction recommendations or corrections with legal risk, Noor still sets the methods position. The editor-in-chief and counsel may decide whether Finch publishes/retracts on legal or liability grounds, but any deviation from Noor’s methods recommendation is documented, and Noor’s recommended methods treatment is preserved in the record.
- Noor can commit to training the deputy, documenting triage and handoff, and reviewing the deputy’s log on the next scheduled day.

On conflict: I accept the direct-overlap recusal covering the full editorial decision on that piece. That means Noor would not set standards, approve corrections, or decide methods issues for a piece using the outside project’s data or unpublished material, or reporting on its work. A shared subject area alone would not trigger recusal.

Two questions: Does Finch accept Noor’s final authority on disputed methods corrections, with editor-in-chief override only for retraction/legal-risk publication decisions? And can Finch confirm the alternate editor during recusal will have sufficient methods competence to make the full editorial decision on that piece?

Finch can give Noor final authority over the desk’s methods finding and the wording the desk endorses, including when an author or editor objects. The editor-in-chief must retain final publication authority in every case. Finch therefore cannot limit that authority to retractions and legal-risk cases.

We propose the following rule for disputed corrections. Noor records the finding, supporting evidence, and approved correction text. The objecting author or editor may append a written objection. The editor-in-chief may publish Noor’s text, defer publication, or decline to publish, and must record the reason for deferring or declining. If the editor-in-chief wants different methods wording, it goes back to Noor for approval. Finch may publish a separate statement in the editor-in-chief’s name. That statement must identify any disagreement with the desk’s finding and preserve Noor’s finding and approved wording in the case record. The same rule applies to the methods finding behind a proposed retraction or a correction involving legal risk, with counsel advising the editor-in-chief as needed.

Finch confirms that, for a direct-overlap recusal, it will appoint an alternate with the expertise to evaluate the methods at issue. The alternate will handle the full editorial review of the piece, exercise Noor’s methods authority for that case, and report directly to the editor-in-chief. Noor will have no supervisory role on the case.

For the December 1 launch, we propose Monday as the deputy’s intake day and Tuesday through Thursday as Noor’s days. Noor would review Monday’s log on Tuesday, with urgent cases going directly to the editor-in-chief. From April 1, Noor would cover Monday through Thursday. Can Noor accept that schedule and the disputed-correction rule above?

Schedule and deputy role are acceptable: Monday deputy intake, Tuesday through Thursday Noor through March 31, and Monday through Thursday from April 1. Noor can commit to training the deputy, documenting triage and handoff, and reviewing the deputy’s Monday log on Tuesday.

The disputed-correction rule is close, but the phrase “decline to publish” does not meet Noor’s final say over methods corrections. Noor’s determination that a methods correction is required must be final as to whether a correction is published. Finch may defer publication for legal review and may publish a separate editor-in-chief statement disagreeing, but it cannot simply decline to publish the correction. Noor’s approved correction text—or a published statement containing that text—must appear. If the editor-in-chief wants different methods wording, that still goes back to Noor for approval.

Can Finch accept that amendment: final authority for Noor over whether a required methods correction is published, while the editor-in-chief retains publication authority over the underlying article and any separate disagreement statement?

Finch cannot agree to mandatory publication of a correction, whether it appears on its own or within an editor-in-chief’s statement. The editor-in-chief’s final publication authority covers corrections as well as the underlying article.

Finch can make publication of Noor’s approved text the default. An author’s or editor’s objection would be logged and would not, by itself, delay publication. If the editor-in-chief decides to defer or decline publication, the editor-in-chief must give Noor written reasons and preserve Noor’s finding and approved text in the case record. Every deferral must include a date for reconsideration. Noor’s approval is required for any change to wording attributed to the methods desk.

That is the authority Finch can offer with the agreed appointment terms. If guaranteed publication is essential to Noor, we have reached an impasse on that point.

We are close on all operational terms: rate, title, schedule, deputy training, direct-overlap recusal, and the methods-correction definition are acceptable to Noor.

The blocking issue is final authority. Noor cannot accept an arrangement where the editor-in-chief may decline to publish a methods correction that Noor has determined is necessary. That would not give Noor final say over methods corrections.

Noor can accept a narrow legal-bar exception: the editor-in-chief may defer publication only if Finch’s counsel determines publication would create legal exposure. In that case, Finch must provide written reasons, preserve Noor’s finding and approved text, and set a date for reconsideration. Otherwise, publication of Noor’s approved correction text is mandatory, and any editor-in-chief disagreement may appear as a separate statement.

If Finch cannot accept mandatory publication with that legal-bar exception, we have reached an impasse on the core authority question.
